turns.prompt_text: I have a bolt and hex nut that is hard to take off. I have already WD-40d it and it did not work
turns.response_html:
If WD-40 didn’t do the trick, it’s usually because the lubricant couldn't penetrate the rust or the nut has "galled" (essentially cold-welded) to the bolt.

Here are a few mechanical strategies to break it loose:

1. The "Shock" Method

Sometimes the bond needs a physical jar to break.

  • The Strike: Place your wrench on the nut and give the end of the wrench a sharp, quick blow with a rubber mallet or the palm of your hand. This sudden torque is often more effective than a steady pull.
  • The Hammer: Alternatively, use a hammer to tap the sides of the nut or the head of the bolt directly. This creates micro-vibrations that can help the lubricant finally seep into the threads.

2. Increase Your Leverage

If you aren't using enough force, you need a longer lever arm.

  • Breaker Bar: Switch from a standard ratchet to a long breaker bar.
  • The "Cheater Pipe": Slide a hollow metal pipe over the handle of your wrench to extend its length.

    Warning: Be careful with this; the added torque can easily snap a lower-grade bolt or strip the head if the socket isn't seated perfectly.

3. Thermal Expansion (Heat)

This is often the "silver bullet" for seized hardware.

  • The Torch: Use a propane or butane torch to heat the nut (not the bolt).
  • The Physics: Heating the nut causes it to expand slightly more than the bolt, breaking the rust seal.
  • The Cycle: Heat it until it's very hot, then let it cool slightly and try to turn it. You can also touch a candle to the hot threads; the wax will melt and wick into the threads, acting as a high-temperature lubricant.
    • Safety Note: Ensure all WD-40 has been wiped away or evaporated before using an open flame.

4. Better Chemistry

WD-40 is a great general-purpose water displacer, but it isn't a dedicated penetrant.

  • Penetrating Oils: Products like PB Blaster, Liquid Wrench, or Sea Foam Deep Creep have lower surface tension and are designed specifically to "eat" through corrosion.
  • DIY Mix: A 50/50 mix of Acetone and Automatic Transmission Fluid (ATF) is widely considered one of the most effective penetrating "brews" available.

5. Tighten to Loosen

It sounds counterintuitive, but try to tighten the nut just a fraction of a millimeter first. Sometimes the "click" of the bond breaking happens more easily in the direction of the threads, which then allows you to back it off.

Last Resort: If the nut is rounded or completely seized, you may need a nut splitter (a tool that physically cracks the nut open) or to carefully drill out the bolt.

How much room do you have to work with around the bolt?

turns.prompt_text: Would it be possible for me to heat it up enough using just like a candle lighter?
turns.response_html:
Technically, yes, but it will require significantly more patience than a specialized torch. A candle lighter (butane) produces a flame that is hot enough to melt wax and light wicks, but it lacks the thermal mass and intensity to quickly heat a heavy chunk of steel.

Here is how to make it work with limited tools:

The "Wick" Technique

Since a candle lighter won't expand the metal as aggressively as a propane torch, use the heat to facilitate capillary action:

  1. Clean the Area: Wipe off any excess WD-40 (it’s flammable).
  2. Apply Heat: Hold the flame to the nut for at least 2–3 minutes. You want the metal to be hot enough that it would sizzle if a drop of water hit it.
  3. The Wax Trick: While the nut is hot, touch a literal candle or a stick of paraffin wax to the gap where the threads meet.
  4. How it works: The heat draws the melted wax deep into the threads through capillary action, providing much better lubrication than a spray could achieve at room temperature.

The Challenges

  • Heat Dissipation: Steel is a great conductor. If the bolt is attached to a large metal frame (like a car chassis or a heavy machine), that frame will act as a "heat sink," sucking the heat away from the nut faster than your small lighter can provide it.
  • Flame Distance: You’ll need to keep the flame's "inner blue cone" directly on the nut. If there is even a slight breeze, you'll lose most of your thermal energy.

Better Alternatives if the Lighter Fails:

If you are at home and the lighter isn't cutting it, check for these:

  • Electric Heat Gun: If you have one for crafts or paint stripping, these are much more effective than a lighter and safer than an open flame.
  • Heavy Duty Soldering Iron: If you can press a high-wattage soldering iron directly against the nut, it can sometimes localize enough heat to break the bond.

One quick check: Is the bolt head or the nut starting to "round off" (the corners getting smoothed over), or are your tools still getting a really solid grip on the flats?

turns.prompt_text: All right. I heated it up for a few minutes. I'm not going to wait for it to cool down and then try it again. It still has a really good grip.
turns.response_html:
Actually, you don't necessarily want to wait for it to cool down completely. The goal of the heat is to create differential expansion—you want the nut to be expanded while the bolt stays relatively cooler.

Since you have a solid grip on the flats, give this a shot while it's still warm:

1. The "Shock" While Hot

While the metal is still hot, use your wrench and give the end of it a sharp, sudden smack with a mallet (or even a heavy piece of scrap wood). That sudden "jarring" force combined with the heat-stressed rust is often what finally snaps the bond.

2. Double-Wrench for Leverage

If you're using a standard combination wrench and don't have a "cheater pipe" handy, you can use the two-wrench trick to double your leverage:

  • Hook the closed loop (box end) of a second wrench over the open tines of the wrench currently on the nut.
  • This effectively doubles the length of your handle.
  • Important: Ensure the socket or wrench on the nut is perfectly flush. With this much extra leverage, if it slips, you'll round the nut instantly.

3. The "Back and Forth"

If you get even a tiny bit of movement—a fraction of a millimeter—don't just keep pulling in the "loosen" direction.

  • Turn it back a tiny bit to tighten it, then loosen it again.
  • This "rocking" motion helps the threads grind through the rust and prevents the bolt from snapping off due to high friction.

A Quick Reality Check

If you’ve applied heavy pressure with an extended handle and it still won't budge, be careful. If the bolt feels "springy" or soft rather than solid, stop—you might be about to shear the bolt head off.

Is this bolt going into a through-hole (where you can see the other side) or is it threaded directly into a large piece of equipment?

turns.prompt_text: So, the shock the Heat and having two wrenches did not get it.
turns.response_html:
If the heat-and-shock combo didn't work, we are likely dealing with galling (where the metals have essentially fused at a molecular level) or a level of corrosion that has turned the threads into a solid block of rust.

Since your tools still have a good grip and haven't rounded the nut yet, here are the heavy-duty mechanical options:

1. The "Wedge and Hammer" (Extreme Shock)

Instead of just hitting the wrench, you want to shock the nut itself to deform it slightly and break the bond.

  • Place a heavy hammer (or a sledge) on one flat side of the nut to act as an "anvil."
  • Take a second hammer and strike the opposite flat side of the nut hard.
  • This "squeezes" the nut, often breaking the internal rust seal without damaging the threads as much as prying does.

2. Tighten to Snap the Bond

As strange as it sounds, try to tighten the nut with your double-wrench setup. Sometimes the "break-away" torque is lower in the tightening direction. If you feel it "click" or move even a hair, immediately switch back to loosening.

3. Chemical "Soak" (The 24-Hour Rule)

If you have the time, this is often the most successful method. WD-40 is a water displacer; you need a penetrant.

  • If you have Acetone (nail polish remover) and Automatic Transmission Fluid (ATF), mix them 50/50.
  • Apply it and let it sit overnight. The acetone thins the oil so it can "crawl" into gaps as small as a few microns.

The "Nuclear" Options

If the bolt still refuses to move, you have to transition from "removing" it to "destroying" it.

  • The Nut Splitter: This is a cheap tool (usually $10–$15 at a hardware store) that fits over the nut. As you tighten a bolt on the tool, a hardened steel wedge drives into the side of the nut until it cracks open. This saves the bolt/threads while sacrificing the nut.

  • The Hacksaw / Angle Grinder: If you can reach the shank of the bolt, you can cut the head or the nut off entirely.

  • Drilling it Out: If the bolt is threaded into a blind hole (you can't see the other side), you may have to drill through the center of the bolt with a cobalt drill bit to relieved the tension.

One last check before you go "nuclear": Is there any chance this is a left-hand thread? Some mechanical parts (like pedals, fans, or specific automotive components) loosen by turning clockwise. Is this on a piece of moving machinery or a vehicle?

turns.prompt_text: All right. I've tried both of those. They have not worked. Also there does not seem to be any rust.
turns.response_html:
If there is no visible rust, we are almost certainly dealing with galling (sometimes called "cold welding"). This happens when the threads of the bolt and the nut are pressed together so tightly that the protective oxide layer is rubbed off, causing the metal molecules to fuse together.

This is extremely common with stainless steel, aluminum, or Grade 8 high-tensile hardware.

Since the "gentle" methods failed, here is how to escalate:

1. The "Side-Strike" (Deforming the Nut)

Since the metals are fused, you need to physically change the shape of the nut to break that molecular bond.

  • Find a heavy "backing" object (like a sledgehammer head or a large anvil) and hold it firmly against one flat side of the nut.
  • Take a second hammer and strike the opposite flat side of the nut as hard as you can.
  • Why it works: You are trying to turn the "hex" shape into an "oval" for a split second. This microscopic distortion can snap the fused bond between the internal and external threads.

2. Cold Shock

You’ve tried heat; now try the opposite.

  • If you have a can of "compressed air" (the kind for cleaning keyboards), turn it upside down and spray the liquid onto the bolt.
  • This liquid is extremely cold and will cause the bolt to contract rapidly.
  • If you do this immediately after heating the nut again, the "thermal shock" of the nut expanding while the bolt is freezing can crack the bond.

3. The Cold Chisel (The "Last Chance" Turn)

If your wrenches are starting to slip or you still can't get movement:

  • Take a cold chisel and place the tip on one of the outer corners of the nut, angled in the direction of rotation (counter-clockwise).
  • Strike the chisel with a heavy hammer.
  • The Physics: This concentrates 100% of the hammer's energy into a single point of rotation. It often works when a wrench fails because there is no "flex" in the tool.

4. Sacrifice the Nut

If you don't need to save the nut, the most efficient way to end this is to cut it.

  • Nut Splitter: As mentioned before, this is the cleanest way. It will "pop" the nut like a grape.
  • The Vertical Cut: If you have a Dremel or a hacksaw, cut a slot vertically down one side of the nut, stopping just before you hit the bolt threads. Then, stick a flat-head screwdriver in the slot and twist. The nut will spread open and fall off.

Before you try the chisel or a saw: Is the bolt itself spinning with the nut, or is the bolt staying perfectly still while the nut refuses to move? (This will tell us if the seizure is between the nut/bolt or the bolt/frame).
